paras: The attempted lynching of Joe Loftin took place at Monticello, Lawrence County, Mississippi, early on Tuesday, August 14, 1888, when about 150 or 200 armed men rode into town to lynch Loftin, an escaped convict held in the county jail. Sheriff D. M. Lee had removed the prisoner the evening before and, by his own account, placed him in the Penitentiary. The sheriff's house was burned that night, and the affair split the county into rival citizens' meetings over whether Lee should resign.

According to the Brookhaven Leader, Loftin had been convicted of murdering his elder brother in 1884 and sentenced to life in the Penitentiary, but escaped from a railroad convict camp and spent more than a year at large in Lawrence County. The paper said he went armed, demanded what he wanted at the houses of people "white and black," threatened witnesses against him, and it tied the recent killing of James E. Sauls to "Loftin's movements."

On Saturday, August 11, B. B. Stringer, whom Lee had deputized to make the arrest, found Loftin at William Russell's house about ten miles from Monticello. The first report said Loftin was fired on by a squad and wounded Leon Branton in the thigh; Stringer, writing to correct "erroneous reports," said he fired first because Loftin had a gun leveled on a boy in his party, who was then shot in the leg. Wounded, Loftin sent for the sheriff, surrendered to him and was taken to the Monticello jail.

On Monday evening, hearing that a mob was being organized, Lee set out with Geo. Garrett and Arthur Fox to carry the prisoner across country to Jackson. Early the next morning about 150 or 200 armed men rode into Monticello to lynch Loftin, and when they found him gone, the Leader wrote, "their anger knew no bounds." That night the sheriff's house was burned while he and his wife were away, and the Leader presumed it was set by "the more extreme of the lynching party."

A citizens' meeting at Monticello on August 14 resolved that Loftin "should have been hanged higher than Haman," accused Lee of disarming citizens at Loftin's request, and asked him to resign. Lee replied in a statement that he had been told the prisoner would be mobbed, that he did not "censure any man for trying to mob him," and that rather than hold Loftin for an infuriated mob he had placed him in the Penitentiary. He called a second citizens' meeting, set for August 25, illegal and asked people to stay away.

On August 22 a mass meeting of about 400 citizens endorsed Lee for removing Loftin "out of reach of a mad and determined mob" and blamed the fire on a "fire fiend" who had taken part in the earlier meeting. The meeting asked Governor Lowry to offer rewards for the killers of Sauls and for whoever burned the sheriff's house. No report of an arrest was found; in September the Leader noted only that Lee, burned out "by an incendiary," would rebuild.

The story was carried by the Brookhaven Leader, which called Lawrence its "sister county," from its first report on August 16 through a brief state news item on September 20. It also printed Stringer's letter, the sheriff's statement and the resolutions of both meetings, so that each side of the local dispute appeared in its own words.

Its editorial called it natural that "the best citizens of the county" had resolved on "visiting summary justice upon Loftin when he was captured," and it blamed the sheriff for his earlier inaction. The same editorial held that Lee had done his sworn duty in protecting the prisoner and that the burning of his house "cannot be justified or condoned on any ground." A week later the paper said Lee's statement and the mass meeting's endorsement placed him "in good shape throughout the Loftin affair." No report names Loftin's race or the race of the men who sought him, and the papers treated the affair as a quarrel over a fugitive convict and a lax sheriff.
The August 14 resolutions said Lee disarmed private citizens at Loftin's request, which Lee called untrue.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Loftin
bases: An armed party of 150 or 200 men rode into Monticello to lynch a prisoner who had been removed from the jail by the sheriff, so the episode is an attempted lynching (A1, A7, A9).

The armed party acted without legal authority and sought to punish an escaped convict, but the sheriff had already taken him away and no report says he was harmed by the mob (A1, A7); no one was killed, so it was an attempt, not a lynching.

The Brookhaven Leader's news report, Sheriff Lee's own statement and the Aug. 22 mass meeting's resolutions independently agree that a mob sought Loftin and that the sheriff removed him (A1, A7, A9), though all appeared in one paper.

accounts.label: Brookhaven Leader news report
accounts.gist: Lofton was fired on by a squad, returned fire and surrendered to the sheriff; on hearing of a mob the sheriff left with him Monday evening, and 150 or 200 armed men rode in early Tuesday to lynch him.

accounts.label: Captor's letter (B. B. Stringer)
accounts.gist: Stringer says he fired first because Loftin had a gun leveled on a boy in his party; Loftin then wounded the boy, and the sheriff took Loftin to jail before Stringer returned.

accounts.label: Sheriff's statement
accounts.gist: Lee says he was reliably informed after two days that Loftin would be mobbed, removed him to the Penitentiary, and returned to find himself homeless; he denies disarming private citizens.

accounts.label: Citizens' meeting of Aug. 14
accounts.gist: The resolutions accuse Lee of neglect and of disarming citizens at Loftin's request, say Loftin should have been hanged, and ask Lee to resign.

accounts.label: Mass meeting of Aug. 22
accounts.gist: About 400 citizens praised Lee for removing Loftin from 'a mad and determined mob' and blamed the burning on a 'fire fiend' who had joined the Aug. 14 meeting.

framing.detail: The Brookhaven Leader called the citizens' resolve on 'summary justice' natural given Loftin's record and blamed the sheriff's earlier inaction, yet held that Lee was right to protect his prisoner and that the burning could not be justified. A week later it said Lee's statement and the mass-meeting endorsement placed him 'in good shape' throughout the affair.
Its first report described the armed men's 'anger knew no bounds' when they found the prisoner gone and later printed both rival meetings' resolutions and the sheriff's statement.
